The Frillfin goby Bathygobius soporator is a small but ecologically significant gobiid fish inhabiting intertidal pools and rocky shorelines throughout the tropical western Atlantic. Under stable laboratory conditions maintained at 27.3 °C [T = 27.3 °C], embryonic development proceeds rapidly, and the chorion ruptures to release a prolarva after just 16 days [ab = 16 days]. This brief incubation period is typical of many small-bodied gobies that spawn in warm, ephemeral tidal habitats where rapid hatching enhances offspring survival. The newly emerged yolk-sac larva carries a modest endowment of endogenous reserves, with a wet weight at birth of only 0.0023 grams [Wwb = 0.0023 grams], reflecting the diminutive egg diameter characteristic of the genus. This lecithotrophic stage relies entirely on yolk absorption before the onset of exogenous feeding, a critical transition that must occur before the point of no return is reached.

Field surveys and mark-recapture studies have provided robust estimates of the species' size structure across its range. The ultimate total length attained by adults is 15 centimeters [Li = 15 centimeters], placing B. soporator among the larger members of its genus but still modest compared to many other intertidal teleosts. Closely related congeneric species, such as Bathygobius fuscus, frequently exhibit similar maximum sizes, suggesting a conserved growth trajectory within the lineage. The corresponding ultimate wet weight for a fully grown individual scales allometrically with length, reaching approximately 34.3 grams [Wwi = approximately 34.3 grams] based on the length-weight relationship observed in local populations. This asymptotic mass is typically achieved after two to three growing seasons, after which somatic growth decelerates markedly as resources are increasingly channeled into reproductive effort.

Sexual maturation in the Frillfin goby is initiated once individuals reach a clearly defined size threshold. The total length at puberty has been determined from histological examination of gonadal tissue and is estimated at 8.2 centimeters [Lp = 8.2 centimeters], a size that corresponds to approximately one-half of the ultimate adult length. The wet weight at puberty, derived from the same length-weight regression, is 5.2 grams [Wwp = 5.2 grams], indicating that reproductive activation commences well before full body size is achieved. This pattern of early maturation relative to asymptotic size is common among small, short-lived gobiids that inhabit unpredictable intertidal environments, where the probability of surviving to a later breeding season is relatively low. The initiation of vitellogenesis and the onset of gametogenesis are thus tightly coupled to reaching this developmental milestone, rather than to chronological age alone.

The gonadosomatic index (GSI) of Bathygobius soporator was assessed from individuals collected during the peak spawning period. Under the prevailing thermal regime of 27.3 °C [T = 27.3 °C], the mean gonadosomatic index in gravid females was 6% [GSI = 6%]. This index suggests that females do not devote an exceptionally large proportion of their somatic tissue to egg production at any single spawning event, consistent with the species' iteroparous life history and the production of multiple clutches across an extended breeding season.

Longevity records from both field-based capture-mark-recapture efforts and continuous laboratory observations indicate that the maximum lifespan of the Frillfin goby is approximately 4.5 years [am = approximately 4.5 years] at a stable water temperature of 27.3 °C [T = 27.3 °C]. This relatively short lifespan is typical of small-bodied gobiids occupying dynamic nearshore habitats, where predation pressure from piscivorous birds and larger fishes is intense, and where physical disturbance from storms and tidal extremes can cause substantial mortality. The lifespan of several related Bathygobius species, including Bathygobius coalitus, has been reported within a similar range of 3 to 5 years, reinforcing the family-wide pattern of rapid maturation, early reproduction, and relatively brief adult life. The combination of early puberty at 8.2 centimeters total length, repeated spawning events, and a maximum longevity of under five years defines a classic fast-paced life history strategy well suited to the challenging ecological conditions of the intertidal zone.
